body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Predictors of failed same-day discharge after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a retrospective analysis of 2,940 procedures","authors":"Achterberg-Kamau P, Lindqvist-Ferreira J, Osei-Whitlock D","year":2017,"venue":"Day Case Outcomes Review","doi":"10.5555/jdso.2017.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 2,940 elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies booked as day cases at two hospitals. Same-day discharge failed in 21 percent. Age over 70, higher anaesthetic risk class, a start after 13:00, nausea needing rescue treatment and placement of a drain were associated with failure. A model with nine predictors had a c statistic of 0.72 in the development data. The model was not validated in other data, the authors selected predictors partly by statistical significance, and several candidate variables had more than 20 percent missing values."},{"title":"Operating list position and same-day discharge after day-case cholecystectomy","authors":"Grieve-Nakashima R, Moreau-Obi T","year":2020,"venue":"Surgical Scheduling Research","doi":"10.5555/ssr.2020.0064","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 1,810 day-case cholecystectomies, same-day discharge failed in 38 percent of operations starting after 14:00 and in 14 percent of those starting before 11:00. After adjustment for patient factors, a start after 14:00 remained strongly associated with overnight stay. Patients placed late on the list were older and had more comorbidities in one of the two hospitals, suggesting that list order was partly chosen by risk. The authors recommend that booking rules consider both patient risk and list position rather than treating list position as fixed."},{"title":"Chart documentation of postoperative nausea and mobilisation after day surgery: agreement with direct observation","authors":"Varadi-Oyelaran K, Petrossian-Holm A","year":2019,"venue":"Perioperative Information Quality","doi":"10.5555/piq.2019.0041","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Trained observers recorded nausea severity and the time of first mobilisation for 420 day surgery patients and compared them with the clinical record. Nausea severity was documented in 41 percent of charts, and the time of first mobilisation in 36 percent. When documented, nausea severity agreed moderately with observation. Administration of a rescue antiemetic was recorded for almost every patient who received one. The authors conclude that charts are a poor source for nausea severity and mobilisation times but that medication records may serve as a proxy."},{"title":"Rescue antiemetic administration as a proxy for postoperative nausea and vomiting in electronic records: a validation study","authors":"Kowalczyk-Adeyemi S, Harcourt-Lund M","year":2022,"venue":"Perioperative Information Quality","doi":"10.5555/piq.2022.0137","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared rescue antiemetic doses recorded in the electronic medication record with nurse-assessed postoperative nausea and vomiting in 1,120 day surgery patients. Agreement for clinically important nausea or vomiting was good (kappa 0.71). The proxy missed patients whose nausea was managed without medication and counted some doses given for prevention after a first episode. Agreement was similar across surgical specialties. The authors suggest the proxy is suitable for research on nausea severe enough to need treatment, but not for mild nausea."},{"title":"Surgeon variation in same-day discharge after laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multilevel analysis","authors":"Ruiz-Mbeki H, Sorensen-Tanaka L","year":2021,"venue":"Day Case Outcomes Review","doi":"10.5555/jdso.2021.0209","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 4,380 day-case cholecystectomies by 31 surgeons, the intraclass correlation for same-day discharge failure at the surgeon level was 0.09 after adjustment for patient factors and list position. Surgeon-level variation was explained partly by drain use and by the timing of the first postoperative review. Surgeons with lower failure rates more often discharged patients directly from the recovery area. The authors recommend accounting for surgeon clustering in prediction and quality work and caution against ranking surgeons on unadjusted rates or small numbers of cases."},{"title":"Prediction models for discharge after day-case surgery: a systematic review of development and validation","authors":"Mistry-Okonkwo A, Castellanos-Brandt E, Nwosu-Lindgren F","year":2023,"venue":"Perioperative Prediction Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ppr.2023.0072","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 14 prediction models for failed discharge after day-case surgery. Eleven were at high risk of bias, most often because of too few events for the number of candidate predictors (median 6 events per candidate predictor), selection of predictors by significance and no correction for optimism. Only three models were validated in data from another period or hospital, and their c statistics fell by 0.05 to 0.11. Calibration was reported for four models. The authors recommend pre-specified predictors, penalised estimation and temporal or external validation."},{"title":"A nurse-led discharge readiness assessment after day surgery: a prospective cohort","authors":"Haddad-Whitfield N, Achebe-Soto R","year":2015,"venue":"Recovery Unit Nursing Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 760 day surgery patients, nurses completed a standard discharge readiness assessment four hours after surgery, covering nausea, pain, mobilisation, voiding and escort. Of patients assessed as ready, 88 percent went home the same day. The assessment took a median of 6 minutes. Patients assessed as not ready most often had nausea or had not yet walked. The assessment required a nurse dedicated to recovery follow-up for the study period, which the unit could not sustain afterwards, and assessments were missed on days when that nurse was absent."},{"title":"Patients' views on same-day discharge after gallbladder surgery","authors":"Lemaire-Ito C, Okafor-Rasmussen D","year":2024,"venue":"Surgical Patient Experience","doi":"10.5555/spe.2024.0033","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 24 patients who had day-case gallbladder surgery, of whom 9 stayed overnight unexpectedly. Patients wanted to know in advance whether an overnight stay was likely so they could arrange transport and care at home. Those converted to an overnight stay late in the evening described frustration and poor sleep on a busy ward. Patients living alone or far from the hospital were most worried about going home the same day. Participants came from one hospital and volunteered after a postal invitation."}]}
